sections.title: What you will learn to say

blocks.text: This lesson is about amounts: how many nuts you need, a little free time you have, too little privacy, two bags of rice. The key question is always: can you count it one by one?

examples.en: How many pecans do we need?
We have a little leisure time.
We have little privacy.
We need two bags of rice.

sections.title: Things you count and things you don't

blocks.text: Some things you count one by one: a bookend, two ottomans — a or an for one, -s after two. Others are a mass or a group word: crockery, gravel, housework. They take no a and no -s.

examples.en: This is a bookend.
There are two ottomans in the room.
This crockery is new.
This is an errand.
This housework is tiring.

fixes.wrong: There are two ottoman in the room.
fixes.right: There are two ottomans in the room.

fixes.wrong: There are a two ottomans in the room.
fixes.right: There are two ottomans in the room.

drill.why: You count peppercorns: -s after two, and no a.

sections.title: many or much — «how many? how much?»

blocks.text: Things you count — many: How many pecans? Things you don't — much: How much polenta? With not too: We don't have much semolina. Never put a before many or much.

examples.en: How many pecans do we need?
How much polenta do we need?
We don't have much semolina.
How many commuters use this train?
How much congestion is there today?

fixes.wrong: How much pecans do we need?
fixes.right: How many pecans do we need?

fixes.wrong: How many polenta do we need?
fixes.right: How much polenta do we need?

fixes.wrong: How a many pecans do we need?
fixes.right: How many pecans do we need?

drill.question: You are counting course assignments — you can count them one by one. How do you ask?
drill.optionA: How much assignments do we have?
drill.optionB: How many assignments do we have?

sections.title: a few, a little — «there is some»

blocks.text: Not much, but there is some: a few for things you count, a little for things you don't. We have a few housemates. We have a little leisure time.

examples.en: We have a few housemates.
We have a little leisure time.
We received a few compliments.
We have a little quinoa.

fixes.wrong: We have a few leisure time.
fixes.right: We have a little leisure time.

blocks.text: Take away a and the meaning changes: less than you would like. We have little privacy. I have few contact numbers. a few / a little — there is some; few / little — not enough.

examples.en: We have little privacy.
We received little encouragement.
I have few contact numbers.
We have little buckwheat left.
I received a few voice messages.

drill.why: Mass and not enough: little, no a.

blocks.text: In a normal sentence use some: We sent some job applications. With not and in questions use any: We don't have any contact details; Do you need any childcare? Both work for things you count and things you don't.

examples.en: We sent some job applications.
We don't have any contact details.
Do you need any childcare?
There aren't any service charges.
Is there any public parking here?

fixes.wrong: We don't have some contact details.
fixes.right: We don't have any contact details.

sections.title: Two bags, two litres: two bags of…

blocks.text: You cannot count a mass in pieces, so count the packs and measures: two bags of rice, two litres of milk, two pieces of advice. The pack takes -s, and of always comes between the pack and the food.

examples.en: We need two tubes of toothpaste.
We need two bars of soap.
We need two bags of rice.
We need two litres of milk.
I need two pieces of advice.

fixes.wrong: We need two tube of toothpaste.
fixes.right: We need two tubes of toothpaste.
We need two tubes of toothpaste.

drill.prompt: Say that you need two jars of jam.

fixes.wrong: How much pecans do we need?
fixes.right: How many pecans do we need?

fixes.wrong: We have a few leisure time.
fixes.right: We have a little leisure time.

fixes.wrong: We don't have some contact details.
fixes.right: We don't have any contact details.
We need two tubes of toothpaste.

blocks.text: First ask: can I count it one by one? Yes — a, -s, many, a few. No — no a, no -s, much, a little, and to count it, a pack with of.
Count — many, a few, few. Mass — much, a little, little. With a — there is some; without a — not enough. Some in normal sentences, any with not and in questions. Pack + s + of.

examples.en: How much knowledge do we need?
I need a little personal space.
We need two slices of cheese.
